evaluated.name: Value_x_Capex_Deceleration
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(capx, at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Discipline is revealed by a *turn* in capital deployment, not its level: cheap firms that are actively cutting capital-expenditure intensity are redirecting cash away from low-return expansion, and this pivot is recognized slowly, whereas expensive firms ramping capex intensity are financing the growth narrative the market has already paid for.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the asset-growth level with the year-over-year change in capex/assets moves the investment leg off the published Cooper-Gulen-Schill variable and onto an investment-policy change that only has return content when combined with where price sits relative to book. Multiplying industry ranks makes the score require both conditions jointly (an industry-cheap firm that is accelerating capex scores near the bottom), and industry ranking neutralizes the large sector differences in capital intensity and book-to-market.

evaluated.name: CashYield_Per_Capital_Intensity
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), ADD(0.05, MA(RATIO(capx, at), 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What investors should pay for is cash flow that does not have to be continuously re-fed with capital: a high EBITDA yield sustained with light, stable capital spending indicates a genuinely underpriced, capital-light franchise, while the same yield requiring heavy ongoing capex is an illusion of cheapness.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are now dimensionless and genuinely dispersed — the three-year average capx/at ranges from near zero to roughly 0.30, so the denominator varies by a factor of about seven and materially reorders firms rather than applying a cosmetic tilt. The 0.05 floor prevents explosive values for near-zero-capex firms and WINSOR trims the residual tails, keeping the ratio economically interpretable as "cash-flow yield per unit of capital the business consumes."

evaluated.hypothesis: Firms trading at rich multiples of sales while aggressively expanding physical capacity — gross plant plus inventory — are building for a demand path the market has already capitalized into price; the combination of a demanding revenue multiple and a capacity build-out predicts disappointment and low subsequent returns.

critic_notes.rationale: This is a plain equal-weight rank blend of two of the most heavily published anomalies (book-to-market and the Cooper-Gulen-Schill asset growth effect) with no conditioning or novel construction, so it is a rediscovery rather than a cross-theme insight.

Because RANK is bounded in [0,1], the denominator only varies between 1 and 2 while the unranked B/M numerator carries the full (fat-tailed) cross-sectional dispersion, so the signal is effectively raw book-to-market with a cosmetic growth tilt.

The sign switch makes the long leg include *expensive* high-asset-growth firms (negative E/P z-score times -1 yields a positive score), which directly contradicts the stated hypothesis and both underlying anomalies, and the switch occurs at the industry mean rather than the claimed median.

Economically coherent and sign-consistent, but the (aqc+sstk)/at leg will be dominated by the well-documented net-share-issuance/composite-issuance anomaly, and the many zero-issuance, zero-acquisition firms create massive rank ties that leave the product's lower half undifferentiated.

The "discipline" term algebraically reduces to (oancf - capx - aqc)/at, i.e. free-cash-flow-to-assets, so the signal is a value-times-cash-flow-quality composite rather than the novel solvency measure claimed, and the hypothesis mislabels what the expression computes.

The firm-relative capital-cycle framing via TS_RANK is a substantively different construction from cross-sectional asset growth and is internally consistent with the stated sign, though it overlaps with the published abnormal-capital-investment effect and the 5-period window yields coarse, tie-heavy values with reduced coverage.

Genuinely distinct from the archive — the enterprise-multiple valuation leg and the acquisition/goodwill-accumulation discipline leg are both economically coherent and only weakly spanned by HML/CMA — though the EV denominator can go near-zero or negative for net-cash firms and should be winsorized or floored before ranking, and the aqc/gdwl COALESCE-to-zero mass will leave a large tied block in the discipline rank.

The framing (own-history rather than cross-sectional) is a legitimately different construction, but TS_RANK of book-to-market over five years is driven almost entirely by the price denominator and is therefore a near-mechanical proxy for the well-documented five-year long-term reversal anomaly, and a 5-point time-series rank is too coarse to sort a cross-section cleanly.

This is a discretized re-expression of the already-tested Value_x_Capex_Deceleration / Expensive_Capacity_Expander mechanism rather than a new one — the proposal's own reasoning concedes it is a diagnostic re-run of the same story — and collapsing to {-1,0,+1} discards information while making leg membership and portfolio composition highly unstable at the z-score cutoffs.

The positive expected sign on high capx/ppent among cheap firms contradicts the well-established capital-investment anomaly (Titman-Wei-Xie), and the stated motivation — that gen-0 alphas came out negative so the orientation should be flipped — is a post-hoc sign fit on the same data rather than an economic mechanism, applied to a trivially simple product of two standard ranks.

The interaction is new to this archive and the working-capital channel is meaningfully distinct from the fixed-capital constructions already tested, but the discipline leg is essentially the Lev-Thiagarajan / Thomas-Zhang inventory-versus-sales fundamental signal, so the burden is on the interaction (not the leg) to add anything, and GROWTH ratios on small or zero inventory bases will need trimming.

A second-moment discipline leg is a genuinely different angle from the archive's level- and change-based capex constructions, but the claim that capex volatility is "uncorrelated by construction" with capex level is simply false (dispersion scales with level, so the leg will partially reproduce a low-investment tilt), and the five-year window plus the earlier EBITDA-yield result suggest coverage and sign risk should be checked before reading much into it.

The centered-rank construction genuinely makes both legs cheap and therefore attacks the archive's diagnosed HML-spanning problem rather than repackaging the same value×investment product, and the expression/sign/hypothesis are internally consistent (long = cheap with flat plant, short = cheap with expanding plant), though "expensive firms held flat" is imprecise since a zero score simply places them in the middle quantiles.

The construction does not do what the reasoning claims — with both legs drawn from heavy investors and the spread running cheap-minus-expensive, it is essentially a plain value spread conditioned on investment and will load heavily on HML, i.e. it maximizes rather than mitigates the very factor-spanning problem the archive diagnosed.

Cumulative five-year acquisition spending is a substantively different (persistence-based) discipline measure than one-year aqc plus goodwill change and the EV floor is a legitimate tail fix, but both changes address measurement noise rather than the actual archived failure (strong FMB slope with essentially zero FF5 alpha), so the alpha problem may well survive.

DELTA(invt/sale) is close to mechanically equivalent to the archived signal's inventory-growth-minus-sales-growth leg (same first-order content, only tail behavior differs), making this a cosmetic variant of an already-evaluated signal rather than a new mechanism.

The hiring-rate return predictability is itself a published anomaly, so novelty rests entirely on the valuation interaction, and emp is a coarse, annually rounded, frequently missing field that will likely depress coverage — but the expression, sign, and hypothesis are consistent and the labor channel is genuinely outside CMA and all capex legs in the archive.

Asset vintage is a legitimately unused, stock-based (and low-cost, high-coverage) construct, but the proposal understates two issues: high ppent/ppegt largely reflects *recent heavy investment*, so the long leg partially contradicts the discipline theme, and vintage is strongly negatively correlated with book-to-market, making the long intersection (cheap plus new plant) thin and the two ranks partly offsetting.

The discipline leg is essentially the accumulated balance-sheet residue of the very same M&A channel already tested twice in the archive (Δgdwl in EVYield_x_Inorganic_Restraint, 5-yr TS_SUM(aqc) in the winning EVYield_x_Serial_Acquirer_History), so it is very likely to be a highly correlated restatement of the existing winner rather than a new mechanism, and goodwill/at is additionally a slow-moving industry/business-model proxy whose "impairment overhang" story is close to published goodwill-impairment work.

A clean single-lever test — swapping the book-equity valuation leg of the archive's marginally significant Value_x_Asset_Vintage for the EV-based multiple that generated the archive's only reliable alpha — with an economically sensible motivation (removing the mechanical B/M–tangibility offset), and asset vintage (ppent/ppegt) is not a canonical published anomaly.

The funding-mix framing is a genuinely distinct leg and the denominator floor is sensible, but ranking Δdebt scaled by investment will in practice be dominated by the sign and size of net debt issuance, so this partially rediscovers the well-documented debt-issuance/external-financing anomaly rather than isolating a pure funding-source-of-investment effect.

Five-year cumulative capex over gross plant is close to a monotone inverse of the ppent/ppegt asset-vintage measure, so this signal predicts the *opposite* sign to the archive's already-positive Value_x_Asset_Vintage result (new plant good there, recently rebuilt plant bad here) without acknowledging or resolving the contradiction, and the leg is otherwise a rescaled long-window investment-rate variable of the type CMA already spans.

A coherent and cheap stock-versus-flow test in the working-capital channel, but the level of inventory-to-sales within industry is a highly persistent business-model/turnover proxy that risks loading on profitability rather than allocation discipline, and zero-inventory firms will pile up in a large tied top rank.

Reframing acquisitiveness as a bounded mix share is a defensible attempt to separate composition from volume, but it changes two things at once relative to the archived winner (mix-scaling *and* reverting the valuation leg from EBITDA/EV back to B/M), so a null result will be uninterpretable, and the large mass of aqc≈0 firms means the long leg will still overlap heavily with the archive's serial-acquirer signal.

Algebraically this is just the archived gen-3 winner minus half its own EV-yield leg (MUL(A,B−0.5) = MUL(A,B) − 0.5A), i.e. a mechanical demeaning variant of an existing signal rather than a new economic mechanism — and the same "center the discipline rank within value" trick was already tried and failed as Discipline_Within_Value_HMLHedged.

Scaling accumulated depreciation by market capitalization turns the "discipline" leg into an inverse asset-to-market value proxy, so NEG(...) systematically favors expensively priced, asset-light firms and partially cancels the EV-yield leg — the expression does not isolate vintage as the hypothesis claims.

A defensible complementarity test of two archived winners' discipline legs with a clear falsifiable prediction, though it is a mechanical blend that risks diluting the stronger vintage leg toward the weaker acquisition leg rather than delivering new economics.

The gross-plant-plus-inventory-to-enterprise-value leg is a genuinely different valuation axis from anything in the archive and is properly industry-ranked, but it sits close to the well-documented assets-to-market value proxy, so novelty rests mainly on the pairing rather than the ingredient.

The hypothesis explicitly requires the *conjunction* of unconsumed plant and low current capex, but SUMRANK averages the two ranks so a mid-build firm with very young plant and heavy spending can still score high — an intersection (product or MIN) would be needed to implement the stated "harvest state."

Coherent, well-scaled, high-coverage level-based leg that is economically distinct from asset age and M&A history, though value interacted with asset turnover is close to the familiar DuPont/quality-value combination and its incremental novelty over published profitability-plus-value evidence is modest.

This is a one-operator measurement tweak (3-year MA on EBITDA) to the archive's flagship EVYield_x_Asset_Vintage with the identical second leg and identical economic story, i.e. exactly the cosmetic variant the objective warns against, and smoothing a three-year EBITDA average will barely change cross-sectional ranks for most firms.

The coverage diagnosis is sensible, but this is a denominator swap on an archived signal and the resulting leg, −(ppegt−ppent)/EBITDA, is close to a monotone re-expression of the flagship's vintage ratio scaled by capital intensity, while EBITDA now enters both legs (numerator of the valuation leg, denominator of the burden leg), so a "restored coverage" improvement would be hard to distinguish from mechanical overlap with the flagship.

This is only a combiner swap (SUMRANK → product) on an archived pairing, which is close to cosmetic, but the diagnosis is credible — the gen-4 version's sign-inconsistent output (FMB −3.21 against FF5 alpha +2.8%) is the classic symptom of rank-averaging admitting single-leg extremists — so enforcing the stated conjunction is a legitimate, interpretable test rather than a fishing variant.

This is the batch's only genuinely new mechanism — a D&A wedge between EV/EBITDA cheapness and earnings-based cheapness, using the flow rather than the stock of consumed capital — though it overlaps materially with the known accruals anomaly (depreciation is a negative accrual, predicting the same sign) and its expected sign is in direct tension with proposal 2's, so the pair should be interpreted jointly and DELTA(ppegt−ppent) should be checked for disposal contamination.

The conditioning question is legitimate, but ppent appears in both the vintage leg (numerator) and the utilization-change leg (denominator), so a firm that simply stops investing mechanically raises sale/ppent while lowering ppent/ppegt — the two legs push against each other by construction, muddying the intended "young plant that is actually being used" conjunction, and the design otherwise recombines the archived Harvest_State and Capital_Productivity_Gain legs.

MIN and MUL of two [0,1] ranks are very highly rank-correlated, so this will reproduce the flagship's sorts almost exactly, making it a near-duplicate that tests an operator nuance too small to yield an interpretable lesson; it also discards the valuation leg entirely for firms whose vintage rank is lower, which is a strong and unmotivated information loss.

This is a mechanical fourth-leg stacking of two already-tested archive triples (vintage+net-cash at +6.0% and vintage+acquisition-abstinence at +4.9%) with no new economic content, and multiplying four [0,1] ranks makes the spread portfolios a thin quadruple-intersection whose composition instability is a more likely source of any alpha change than the claimed incremental mechanism.

A defensible horse-race that swaps the vintage leg for the renewal-adequacy leg inside the archive's best triple, but the two capital-consumption measures share the same (ppegt−ppent) numerator and are highly collinear, so the test is likely to be a near-duplicate of the +6.0% signal rather than a substantively different construction.

Net debt already sits in the EV-yield denominator, so the two legs are mechanically correlated and the "interaction" is largely a nonlinear re-weighting of one variable; moreover scaling net debt by gross plant injects capital intensity rather than financing discipline (asset-light firms are penalized by construction), and value-times-leverage is close to well-documented distress/leverage territory.

The best-constructed proposal here: it turns the archive's strongest mechanism into a single, economically interpretable multiple with an internally consistent sign (young plant → small accumulated depreciation → higher yield), high coverage, and a genuine discriminating prediction versus the flow-based version that failed, though the reviewer should check that it does not collapse into a mechanical EBITDA-to-gross-capital profitability ranking.

Extending the "standing claims" logic to working capital is a legitimately distinct dimension rather than a relabelled one, but it repeats the archive's now-standard triple-rank-product template and the inventory/sales leg was already weak as a value partner, so expectations for incremental alpha should be modest.

The expression does not compute what the hypothesis claims — gross PPE is a cumulative stock that rarely declines, so a five-year low in ppegt/sale is overwhelmingly driven by rising sales rather than capacity rationalization, making this largely a sales-growth (and by extension low-asset-growth) proxy interacted with value; the 5-point TS_RANK on annual data is also very coarse.

A clean, well-motivated ablation that isolates whether the winner's power comes from "deferred renewal" or simply from cash-per-unit-of-capital-intensity, but be aware that cash/gross-PPE is close to a cash-to-assets screen, so a comparable result would suggest the family is largely a rediscovery of the cash-holdings premium interacted with value rather than a claims-theory effect.

Economically sensible and internally consistent, but it is a third denominator swap on the same cash leg and carries almost the same diagnostic content as Signal 1 — running both in one generation yields little incremental information, and if all three deflators perform alike the honest conclusion is that only the cash numerator matters.

The two legs are genuinely distinct (balance-sheet funding vs operating-model working capital) and the expression matches the hypothesis, but multiplying the archive's two highest-alpha legs is a greedy in-sample recombination whose apparent improvement should be discounted for selection bias and for the corner-concentration of a triple rank product.

Consolidating the separate claim legs into a single dollar-denominated coverage ratio is a substantively different construction that allows offsetting across claims and directly tests the claims theory against the "stacked conservative screens" alternative, though note that ebitda enters both legs and that the denominator is likely dominated by debt, so the leg may largely reproduce the known low-leverage/net-cash effect.

Applying a three-year moving average to the winning leg is the archetypal cosmetic refinement — the turnover and transitory-liquidity rationale is plausible but weak, and the near-certain outcome is a slightly attenuated version of the same signal that teaches little about the mechanism.

This is exactly the right skeptical test: cash lowers net EV and simultaneously raises the pre-funding leg, so the archive's headline +7% alpha is partly suspect as a mechanical double-count, and stripping the cash netting from the valuation leg is the decisive, low-cost diagnostic that should precede any further building on that construction.

This is the archive's EVYield_x_Prefunded_But_Not_Deploying with net EV mechanically swapped for gross EV — a deflator tweak whose effect has already been established separately by GrossEVYield_x_Prefunded_Replacement_Bill, so it is a cosmetic variant rather than a new economic question.

A defensible cash-free ablation of the claims mechanism with coherent sign and high coverage, though scaling accumulated depreciation by total assets converts it partly into an asset-light/capital-intensity tilt (and overlaps the already-tested ppent/ppegt vintage leg), a confound the proposal does not acknowledge.

Swapping the valuation axis is a low-novelty edit, but it is a genuine and cleanly specified attribution test of whether the pre-funding interaction requires a cash-flow multiple, and the authors correctly pre-commit to interpreting a weak result as informative.

Self-described as a "robustness re-test" of an already-evaluated triple (EVYield_x_Prefunded_Bill_And_Lean_Inventory, +6.6%, t=5.75) with only the EV denominator altered — the double-count fix has already been validated once, so this adds little beyond a duplicate.

The reasoning claims this "extends the mechanism to a different claim rather than re-deflating the same one," but it is precisely a third re-deflation of the same cash numerator (after che/(ppegt−ppent) and che/ppegt, which already delivered near-identical ~6–7% alphas), so it mostly re-measures the cash-holdings tilt under a new scaler.

This is the batch's only substantively new economic dimension — conditioning the liquidity/optionality state on demonstrated realised return per dollar deployed — with a coherent agency rationale and correct expected sign, though the shared ebitda term across legs and the three-way rank product's coverage cost warrant careful diagnosis.

This is the gen-7 EVYield_x_Prefunded_But_Not_Deploying signal with the valuation leg swapped from net to gross EV — a substitution the archive already showed to be immaterial (0.070/t=5.82 vs 0.071/t=5.85 in the two-leg pair) — so it is a cosmetic variant rather than a new economic hypothesis.

A fourth denominator ablation of the same prefunding interaction (net EV, gross EV, and book equity already tested) offers negligible incremental information, and dropping debt from the denominator makes leverage a hidden driver of the "cheapness" leg, which sits awkwardly with a hypothesis about unencumbered cash flow.

The only new content is cumulative five-year equity issuance scaled by market cap, which is essentially the well-documented net/composite share-issuance anomaly (Pontiff–Woodgate, Daniel–Titman) and will likely dominate the triple, so any improvement would be attributable to a known effect rather than to the funding-history mechanism claimed.

The two discipline legs are close to algebraically redundant with the existing prefunding ratio — multiplying (deployment/cash)⁻¹ by (consumed capital/assets)⁻¹ largely reconstructs cash-over-consumed-capital scaled by deployment — so this is near-collinear with the +7% archive winners rather than a genuinely independent construction.

Distribution policy as a governance qualifier on the liquidity state is the one economically distinct dimension in this batch (the archive's failed payout test used a reinvestment-share construction, not payout intensity conditioned on prefunding), though the reviewer should watch for rank compression from the mass of zero-dividend firms and a resulting large-cap/quality tilt.

Value crossed with low investment intensity is the classic asset-growth/investment anomaly interacted with book-to-market — largely spanned by the CMA and HML legs of the FF5 benchmark itself — and the archive already contains multiple value-times-capex-restraint variants, so as a signal (as opposed to an internal ablation) it is too well known and too trivial to warrant a slot.
